summary:
Bangladesh presents a high risk for trans visitors. Protests forced the ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, and in the year after that change LGBTQ people faced increased vulnerability to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

Hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground after the 2024 change. Trans people who had previously lived visibly were reported to be living in hiding.

The current national incident baseline is 260 documented human rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across Bangladesh in 2025. The conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. The monitoring group JMBF, in its annual report published in April 2026, describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused.

Section 377 of the Penal Code on unnatural offences provides that whoever voluntarily has carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any man, woman or animal shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Penetration is sufficient to constitute the offence. Its ambit extends to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual heterosexual fellatio and anal penetration. Parliament refused to overturn Section 377 in 2009 and 2013. Formal laws imposed in 1860 through the Indian Penal Code effective in 1862 were carried into the Pakistan Penal Code after the 1947 partition and retained in the legal code since 1971 independence.

It remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within Section 377. A foreign government country policy note of September 2023, updated in April 2026, records that ambiguity, noting that one international review read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to all genders.

The law is rarely enforced through prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ, including extortion and bullying of LGBTI individuals and those considered effeminate. Police have also used a suspicious behavior provision of the police code and have limited registration of LGBTI organizations.

Hijras have been legally recognised as a separate third gender alongside males and females since a cabinet meeting on 11 November 2013. Voter lists offer third gender options, and hijra candidates have run for government positions. In April 2019 hijra was introduced as a third gender option on voting forms for the first time to allow voting under proper gender identity. There are no policies outlining measures individuals must undergo to legally change gender on official documents, no clarity about who may qualify as a hijra, and no protections from discrimination for hijra. Other transgender communities beyond hijras remain unrecognised and unprotected from discrimination.

Extortion driven police violence affects visibly trans people. After hijras refused police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate carrying vehicles in Narayanganj, a traditional livelihood.

Policing reaches transit hubs. In April 2024 five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, as documented by JMBF.

Asylum grade country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues. Members have received threatening messages by telephone, text and social media, with some harassed by police.

Bangladeshi law does not recognise same sex relationships, civil unions or domestic partnership, and does not provide any adoption route for same sex couples. Same sex couples have been detained and can face imprisonment or fine. Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors. There are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
In May 2017, as cited in a 2017 report, armed forces raided the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner. About 120 people present were separated into small groups and beaten. Twenty eight were arrested on suspicion of homosexual activity while media were allowed to photograph some. Authorities later claimed arrest for narcotics possession, with four remanded, twelve detained for questioning and twelve sent directly to jail.

Following that raid and continued harassment, many members including leadership reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, which severely weakened advocacy and support networks. Organizations specifically assisting lesbians are rare. The transgender population, long a marginalized but recognised part of society, faced continued high levels of fear, harassment and law enforcement contact after violent extremist attacks against vulnerable communities.

A school textbook dispute in 2024 illustrates public hostility. On 19 January 2024 part time university lecturer Asif Mahtab Utsha publicly tore the seventh grade History and Social Science textbook story Sharifar Golpo, in which Sharif born male later identifies as woman Sharifa living as hijra, claiming it promotes homosexual and transgender concepts. Student protests followed with statements saying no to LGBTQ and calls for class boycott. He was removed from lectures. A five member Education Ministry review found nineteen words incompatible with Bangladeshi society four months later and recommended omission.

Transgender students have faced exclusion in higher education. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam was excluded from the North South University womens carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest and exam boycott, with rally banners expressing no transgender sentiments. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, a final year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on stated grounds of online threats and carrying a weapon causing fear, which she denied as following her sharing a satirical caricature involving Asif Mahtab Utsha and Dr. Mohammad Sorowar Hossain.

Pride events involving LGBTIQ and hijra people have been held, which indicates limited prior public organizing despite the current hostile climate.
localsOnly:
In December 2014 the Ministry of Social Welfare invited hijras to apply for government employment. In January 2015 the Ministry of Health issued a memorandum requesting steps to identify hijras by conducting thorough medical check ups that required hijras to strip and have genitals confirmed, with photographs later released to confirm hijras are really men.

In July 2015 after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators the government announced plans to recruit and enlist hijras as traffic police.

A government housing scheme for homeless or landless individuals includes transgender people for the first time, with at least 140 transgender community members provided government built houses across the country.

Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka with classes starting 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects for free with no age limit.

Hijras continue to face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care. While hijras are generally more accepted and have historically held culturally important roles, access to social services remains unequal. Social stigma against HIV and AIDS and higher risk populations can be a barrier for accessing health services, especially for the transgender community and men who have sex with men. A Ministry of Social Welfare survey counted 10,000 registered hijras as of 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa treatment of trans visitors, including how foreign passports with changed gender markers are assessed at the border, is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved.

Rules on access to sex segregated facilities, screening procedures that could risk outing, and access to gender affirming care for visitors are not sourced and remain unresolved.

Current prosecution counts and conviction rates under Section 377, beyond the finding of rare enforcement with use for harassment and extortion, are not sourced and remain unresolved.
